passages.source: In AnimatLab, Morrow and I tuned our first walker by changing currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters by hand and running the model again. Each motor neuron recruits a muscle, the muscle pulls on the limb, and sensory signals from the moving limb return to the circuit. A change in any part of that loop can alter the next step. Runs with the older solver were slow enough to make hand tuning impractical for a large parameter search. I wanted to change the controller or the leg geometry, repeat the same test, and identify where the response changed.

For a course project in neuromechanical modeling, Morrow and I coupled the sagittal-plane biped of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} to the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. A shared rhythm generator (RG) drove pattern-formation (PF) pathways and motor neurons (MNs) on both sides. Antagonist Hill-type muscles acted on the thighs, shanks, and feet. I added a passive toe joint. Hunt and I reported the suspended model in a poster for the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}. Its legs cycled in suspension and the model tipped when released toward the ground (Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture}).
\textbf{(A)}\\[2pt]
\textbf{(B)}\\[2pt]
\caption[Original controller-transfer experiment]{The AnimatLab walker assembled by Morrow and Bolen cycled its legs in suspension (A) and tipped when released for the ground test (B).}

The fall left three plausible explanations. An extensor could receive its command too late, produce too little force, or act through too small a moment arm. Changing the muscle attachment could also alter the stretch signal returned to the circuit. To distinguish these effects, I needed the neural command, actuator force, joint motion, and sensory current from the same trial on a common clock.

I used MuJoCo to calculate movement and contact and SNS-Toolbox to evaluate the synthetic nervous system (SNS) \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. I connected the two in scripts so that I could save a controller, change one parameter or pathway, and repeat a trial under the same mechanical conditions. In a later walker model, W2L, the bilateral circuits received heel and toe contact signals from the simulated feet during supported treadmill stepping. I could turn off selected pathways and measure whether the two feet still alternated under load.

I prepared two further kinds of mechanical model (Figure~\ref{fig:simulation_workflow}). For the human reference and its rerouted robot counterpart, I started with muscle paths in OpenSim \citep{delp_opensim_2007,caggiano_myosuite_2022}. For the robot we designed in the lab, I started with its SOLIDWORKS assembly. Both routes let me apply a neural command and measure what the chosen body did with it. Table~\ref{tab:sns_model_configurations} identifies the models in the order I introduce them.

The lower route starts with the robot CAD and uses my import and SNS-Simscape tools. The MathWorks bridge exchanges signals between Simulink and an executable MuJoCo model. The center column identifies my additions to each route.}

Mechanical model & Actuation and controller & Experimental use \\

W2L walker in MuJoCo & Leg muscle actuators and bilateral circuits with contact feedback & Test footfall coordination on a supported treadmill. \\

I used MyoConverter \citep{wang_myosim_2022} to convert the human reference, \path{gait2392_simbody.osim}, then drove its biological-muscle actuators in MuJoCo with a neural controller. Before fitting a circuit, I restored missing maximum-force scales from the OpenSim source and checked that a pull on each tested muscle moved the joint in the intended direction. The model retains 92 actuator entries, including six small hip rotators that remain disabled, and the OpenSim convention of negative knee flexion. I moved each joint through its range to check changes in moment arm at moving points and wrap surfaces, and checked that ground forces arose from foot contact (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_conversion_repairs}).

At matched poses and OpenSim static-optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles gave force-prediction $R^2$ values of 0.88--0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. For those muscles, the mean reference force predicted the sampled force better than the converted model did. This comparison prescribed a pose and activation for each frame. Movement velocity and tendon dynamics were outside its scope.

I next used \path{gait2392_robotbody.osim} to represent the routes proposed for the robot. In my earlier design I had moved actuator origins, insertions, and via points to respect the usable BPA contraction and avoid interference \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,morrow_optimization_2020}. My preparation script mirrored the intended right-side routes to the left and wrote \path{gait2392_robot.osim} for conversion. Applying human muscle parameters to the new paths caused equilibrium failures because the routed lengths had changed. With converted Hill-type actuators, the robot model cycled its legs in suspension. To test a BPA on the same geometry, I supplied a separate force law.

For BPA actuation, my interface evaluates the quasi-static force law from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} at the current routed length and commanded pressure and applies tensile force along the route. This allows a researcher to change the force law while retaining the mechanical geometry. The calculation assumes that commanded pressure is available at the actuator. Valve filling and loading-history effects require separate measurements.

The rerouted OpenSim model let me change where an artificial muscle pulled. Testing the four-bar knee and the mass distribution of our own robot required the geometry of the mechanism we had designed (Chapters~\ref{ch:background} and~\ref{ch:torque}). I used the link and attachment geometry from that earlier CAD work to assemble a mechanical model in MuJoCo. I could also import a CAD mechanism into Simscape Multibody for a Simulink experiment. The MathWorks bridge requires an executable MuJoCo model for tests that use MuJoCo mechanics.

I placed the CAD assembly in its anatomical frame ($x$ anterior, $y$ superior, and $z$ right) using a reference datum, assigned link masses and inertias, and retained the four-bar knee constraints. Actuator tension times a route's signed moment arm gives its joint torque. By virtual work, the moment arm is the negative derivative of route length with respect to joint angle, including the motion of attachment and via points. I checked this derivative by perturbing the angle with the same points active and recorded switches of conditional points separately.

I kept the actuator choice explicit when testing the CAD model. In the supported stepping experiment an engineering controller distributed reference tensions among 54 actuators while the SNS set their timing. This let me test whether one foot accepted load while the other unloaded and cleared the ground. The pressure-dependent BPA interface serves a different experiment, in which the available tension depends on the commanded pressure and current route length.

The full W2Lvar controller for the Gait2392 human model had 888 neurons and 7,868 connected neuron pairs. To change how a knee extensor is recruited, I need to identify the neurons that feed its motor pool and inspect their synaptic parameters. I built graphical tools that let me work on that part of the circuit by function. Scripts assemble repeated connections and run parameter trials. Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives the entry points for the mechanical, neural, and fitting tools.

I implemented the SNS-Simscape library as editable Simulink blocks for neurons, synapses, sensory encoding, activation, and actuator force (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}). The graded equations follow SNS-Toolbox \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Each synapse sends a conductance and its product with reversal potential to the postsynaptic neuron. This makes the sign and strength of a connection available for inspection. From the \path{Code/Matlab/SNS_Simscape/gui} directory, running \verb|app = SNSGui()| opens my circuit editor. A user can place and connect graded neurons, save the circuit description, and generate a Simulink circuit through \path{sns_build_from_json.m}. Separate builders connect complete reflex circuits to the knee and arm dynamics.

\caption[Editable SNS-Simscape blocks]{The twelve SNS-Simscape library elements for constructing neural pathways, encoding sensory measurements, and calculating activation and actuator force. The editable blocks connect these operations through stated signal interfaces.}

{\interlinepenalty=10000 When choosing a sensory connection, I use the SADb to check which afferents an experiment stimulated, which motor population responded, and under what conditions (Chapter~\ref{ch:database}). Those observations guide my choice of the connection's sign and target. To implement it, I choose the mechanical quantity that supplies the model input and set the synapse's operating range. A pulse to an input that projects to an MN tests recruitment. A projection to the PF or RG layer can also change when the next motor burst occurs.\par}

In the reduced knee, extensor and flexor MN outputs pass through activation dynamics to antagonist tensile actuators. Their moments change the knee angle and angular velocity. The spindle-like transducers use joint motion to produce Ia currents, and the Ib transducers use actuator tension. Each Ia pathway excites its own MN and inhibits the antagonist. Each Ib pathway inhibits its own MN. The resulting six connections close the loop that the worked example tests. The Gait2392 and W2L experiments use different sensory encoders and input ports, identified in Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts}.

A researcher can reproduce the knee experiment with \path{run_transient.m} and the archived \texttt{KneeReflexDemo} model. The driver runs the settled knee twice and adds a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} pulse to the extensor Ia current in one run. The pulse recruited the extensor MN. The flexor was already inactive, so the rise in extensor force accounted for the initial extension (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_reflex_current}). The stimulated knee extended \ang{1.09} relative to the control, peaked \qty{111}{\milli\second} after pulse onset, and met the angle and speed recovery criteria \qty{6.355}{\second} after onset. Broader MN and Ia synaptic operating ranges allowed the model to settle before the pulse. The original narrow ranges produced sustained oscillation. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_knee_transient} gives the MATLAB command and the fields to inspect in the saved summary.

\caption[Transient knee feedback response]{The knee circuit (A) receives a \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{30}{\milli\second} extensor Ia pulse (B). Stimulated and control knee angles (C) and motor-neuron activity (D) share the dashed onset line. The left column shows recovery in seconds and the right enlarges onset in milliseconds. Flexion is negative.}

The loaded-cup model uses the pressure-dependent BPA20 force block in the arm. Increasing the simulated cup mass to \qty{0.625}{\kilogram} over \qty{10}{\second} produced \ang{7.85} of sag with feedback disabled and \ang{2.00} with the graded feedback circuit enabled (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_beverage_current}). The matched spiking circuit gave \ang{1.78} at the same ramp endpoint (Appendix~\ref{sec:spiking_results}). As the arm descended, biceps stretch recruited the biceps and inhibited its antagonist. This reduced the sag while the load was still increasing.

\caption[Loaded-cup feedback comparison]{Feedback circuit (A), arm geometry (B), load ramp (C), elevation response (D), and normalized pressure command (E). The BPA20 block supplies actuator force. The \qty{10}{\second} endpoint compares responses during increasing load, rather than equilibrium sag.}

Figure~\ref{fig:sns_design_fit_workflow}A follows two connections in the saved left-leg W2L circuit. One PF neuron excites the extensor motor pool and the other excites the flexor pool. Moving an attachment in CAD can change its moment arm. In a model with length feedback, it can also change the stretch signal returned to the circuit. To test such a revision, I would update the attachment and its actuator and sensor mapping, then run both models with the same saved circuit, external drive, and load. Comparing their actuator forces and joint angles would show how the change affected the closed-loop response.

For experiments with MuJoCo mechanics, I integrated the blocks with the MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink bridge and adapted initialization and sensor readback. A Simulink controller sends an ordered actuator-command array to MuJoCo and reads the resulting joint and actuator measurements. I tested a command source updated every \qty{1}{\milli\second} with a mechanical and sensor update every \qty{5}{\milli\second}. The separate Gait2392 neural and mechanical experiments used \qty{2}{\milli\second} updates.

The bridge delivered the prescribed muscle commands from Simulink to MuJoCo. All five tested sensor arrays matched Python readback bit for bit over 80 steps from \qty{0.005}{\second} through \qty{0.400}{\second}. An exported neural circuit drove all 92 actuator channels for \qty{5}{\second}. A separate reflex test returned mechanical measurements to the controller. Its length encoder saturated after initialization, so the experiment demonstrates bidirectional signal exchange while leaving sensitivity to length untested (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_signal_contracts}).

A successful interface still leaves a question about the circuit it carries. Under constant drive, one Simulink realization settled to a steady voltage while its NumPy reference oscillated. A larger export matched the early transient and diverged later. Comparing neural traces under common inputs localized these discrepancies before the mechanics complicated their interpretation (Appendix~\ref{sec:sns_ports}).

A contact-driven W2L test compared a 26-neuron Simulink rhythm core with the corresponding four RG signals in the 95-neuron NumPy network. With identical drive and prescribed heel inputs, both produced all ten expected bursts with a \qty{1.000}{\second} period over \qtyrange{2}{12}{\second}. The four best-lag voltage correlations were at least 0.99996 with a \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative alignment (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing phasic heel input caused both circuits to latch. The comparison verifies the shared rhythm-generating pathways under this stimulus.

With a circuit and mechanical model that I could run from a script, I replaced hand tuning with a sequence of parameter searches (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_design_fit_workflow}B). I chose a measurable target for one function, set bounds on the parameters that could affect it, ran the candidates, and tested the selected settings again. The target changed as I progressed from rhythm generation to muscle recruitment and then to a loaded movement.

I specify the function of a neural pathway before fitting it. For a PF channel, the target includes the part of the cycle during which the channel should drive its MNs, the duration of that drive, and its overlap with neighboring channels. The test therefore examines the activity transmitted through its synapse. Voltage below the synapse's operating range can vary without changing motor recruitment. Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations} describes the graded and spiking formulations.

I adapted the four calibration operations presented by \citet{hunt_inrc_2019}. I set the intrinsic period to approximately twice the target locomotor period, tuned entrainment under expected afferent input, fitted feedforward motor recruitment, and refined the pattern with sensory feedback. The recruitment targets came from inverse mechanics applied to reference motion. Agreement with those targets measures how well the network reproduces the estimated activation pattern.

For repeated searches I used bounded parameters, tied left and right homologues where symmetry was intended, and used tree-structured Parzen estimation to select candidates. The scripts save parameters, objective components, and the termination condition. A promising candidate is rerun in a fresh process with its fitted parameters before an intervention is introduced.

My physical test sequence changes the loads and sensory information available to the same candidate (Table~\ref{tab:sns_curriculum}). In air, a researcher can tune recruitment and timing before foot contact introduces another source of feedback. Standing and supported stepping then test whether the model carries load and transfers it between its feet. The evaluation scripts reload the saved candidate for each condition.

A result advances a particular controller and mechanical model. A good fit to an MN target can coexist with a timing error upstream, and suspended joint motion can coexist with poor weight transfer. I therefore tested the PF signals before interpreting a motor fit and tested foot loading separately from joint cycling.

Acceptance begins with finite states, completion of the prescribed duration, and protected joint bounds. Suspended experiments assess meaningful joint excursion, cadence, and bilateral phase. Vertical lift, horizontal guidance, and attitude restraint are reported separately because reducing one does not remove the others. A nominal support setting is therefore insufficient to characterize the loading experienced by the model.

A muscle-force comparison can identify a mechanical discrepancy before neural parameters are adjusted. The knee and cup experiments then show what changes when sensory current reaches a motor pool in a model whose load and actuator law are known. By the time a foot touches the treadmill, the same comparison requires a record of contact, actuator force, and external assistance. The progression from one joint to a supported biped makes it possible to ask which part of the loop accounts for a change in behavior.

The W2L sensory intervention illustrates the value of separate outcome measures. All three conditions produced forward movement, but heel-strike phase fell outside the accepted range only after the combined removal. In syn6, an acceptable pattern of motor recruitment likewise concealed a PF channel that remained active throughout the cycle. Recording the signal at the receiving layer distinguished a successful output fit from a circuit that performed its intended function.

The human drive-weaning experiment separated a particular descending input from the mechanical assistance. The human model continued to step in place under its support rig when supplementary left and right drive reached zero. The shared descending input remained active. In a separate W2L robot experiment the model progressed with reduced supplementary drive while the harness remained engaged (Appendix~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}).

Suspension removes ground loading. Rails and guides permit contact but carry part of the weight and constrain motion. The evidence for the BiW2Lvar+ air stages, the W2L pathway removal, W2L108 treadmill stepping, and the CAD model's contact handover therefore applies to four distinct experimental conditions. No experiment in this program established harness-free walking.

The force law also determines what a controller test can establish. The simplified knee actuator isolates the response to a sensory pulse. The BPA20 arm model tests whether the feedback circuit can recruit enough pressure-dependent force as a load increases. Specifying ideal tensions on the CAD model isolates the demands of contact and swing clearance. Applying its controller to physical BPAs introduces a further question about attainable force at each measured length and pressure.

The syn6 result motivates a specific transfer experiment. Record the same PF channel first under prescribed sensory input and then during closed-loop motion. Compare the timing of transmitted output and the knee state when the two responses diverge. This would distinguish a failure of the neural timing circuit under altered input from a mechanical limit that a well-timed command cannot avoid.

For a muscle with poor matched-pose force agreement, I would prescribe the same joint motion and activation history with a rigid tendon and with a compliant tendon, then compare the force traces. I could then vary the activation history while holding the motion and tendon properties fixed. For the robot model, the corresponding experiment would apply a measured pressure history to a characterized BPA route. Repeating a contact or controller test on the repaired model would then show whether the mechanical change affected coordination.

Recorded signals can exercise the embedded sensory encoder, command exchange, and watchdog before connecting valves. A hardware test still requires integrating the compiled SNS binding with physical I/O (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_embedded_interfaces}). Chapter~\ref{ch:overall} connects this test to the actuator and knee measurements.

Restoring the Gait2392 muscle-force scales gave me a human reference for recruitment tests. The BPA model predicts tension from pressure and routed length. In the same \qty{16}{\second} Gait2392 trial, sparse neural execution cut the wall time for the full process from \qty{199.624}{\second} to \qty{29.284}{\second}. A future researcher can edit a pathway or muscle route, fit the controller, and repeat the same test to measure the change in force and motion.

Designing a robot knee for human-scale torque sets two different tests. With the joint fixed, the actuator and its route must transmit the required moment to the shank. During a step, the controller must recruit that actuator while the leg is in a position to accept or release load. A knee can meet the first requirement and still fail the second. The same distinction matters when using a robot to study biology. A change in foot loading after a sensory pathway is disabled has an interpretable cause only when the actuator, route, and external support are known.

I addressed these questions at four points in the design process. The actuator tests show how much tension a BPA of a given resting length can produce at a specified pressure and contraction. At the knee, that tension acts through a moment arm. The isometric tests showed how deflection under load changes the torque available from a proposed route. For controller design, I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) so a researcher can find the experiment behind a proposed feedback connection. The neuromechanical tools then let the researcher change that connection in a model and measure its effect on movement. Figure~\ref{fig:design_workflow} shows where each result enters a new design.

Festo's sizing tool predicted that a shorter BPA would produce greater maximum force. On our isometric test jig, shorter actuators of the same diameter produced less maximum force at \qty{620}{\kPa} (Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles}, Figure~\ref{fig:Fmax_fit}). We used this measured dependence on resting length to scale a three-coefficient force surface fitted to normalized pressure and contraction. A designer can use the model to compare candidate actuator lengths at the pressure and contraction required by a joint, within the range we tested.

For a new actuator, free contraction at the reference pressure, $\varepsilon_{620}$, still has to be measured. The \qty{20}{\mm} specimens came from one batch. Testing several resting lengths within each batch and repeating the series across the \qtylist{10;20;40}{\mm} sizes would distinguish a length trend from manufacturing variation.

One explanation for the resting-length effect concerns the shape of the pressurized tube. Near each end fitting the outer diameter remains close to its uninflated value. It increases through a transition region to the nominal inflated diameter in the central span (Figure~\ref{fig:bpa_construction}A). If the transition occupies a similar axial length at a given pressure, a shorter actuator has a smaller fraction of its wall operating as a uniform cylinder. The physical end cap raises a different question. Measuring relative displacement across Onyx and aluminum caps under matched tensile loads, with the actuator pressurized and unpressurized, would isolate the contribution of cap and attachment compliance. An axial profile of tube diameter is needed to test the transition-region explanation.

Can deformation near the fittings account for the difference in isometric force between short and long actuators? I propose a geometrically nonlinear finite-element model for this question. Festo describes a pressure-sealing rubber wall reinforced by aramid fabric \citep[p.~2]{festo_2026}. I would represent the wall as a nearly incompressible hyperelastic material and the braid as two embedded families of tension-only truss elements following the measured fiber angles. A curved membrane can represent the taut central span when bending is negligible. A thin shell adds bending where curvature varies over distances large compared with wall thickness. A thick shell can represent transverse shear in a shorter transition, while mixed displacement--pressure solids through the thickness are appropriate where the fitting compresses the rubber or produces local contact stress. A flat plate would discard the circumferential load path. I would embed the fibers where they are bonded to the rubber and use measured frictional contact at a mechanically clamped interface that can slip. Sectioning a specimen and marking the wall relative to the fitting would distinguish bonded regions from sliding surfaces. Pressure would follow the deforming inner wall, with the closed-end pressure resultant included once, as the tube expands and the fiber angles change.

I would prescribe the same measured gauge-pressure ramp from zero to \qty{500}{\kPa} for two quasi-static tests, fixing the upper fitting in both. For free contraction the lower fitting would translate along the axis with its fixture weight counterbalanced. For loaded contraction it would lift a known suspended mass with axial load $mg$, including the moving fixture in $m$. At each pressure plateau I would measure fitting separation, the diameter profile along the tube, and axial force at the fixed support. A third test would hold fitting separation fixed and measure the change in reaction with pressure. Agreement in the axial profile and the held-length force across resting lengths would test the end-effect hypothesis directly. Dynamic loading would then address a separate question about pressure response and hysteresis \citep{elzein_pressure_2025}. Appendix~\ref{app:muscle_calcs} gives the biological-muscle formulations used for comparison \citep{thelen_adjustment_2003,millard_flexing_2013}.

On the biomimetic knee, the original rigid-body model overpredicted the torque from the extensor route (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}). I accounted for length offsets, compliance in the loaded force path, and the loss of usable BPA length where it wraps. The fitted stiffness pair includes the compliance of the fixtures and the loading connection. I then used the corrected model to size two routes and tested them on the knee. At the sampled angles, the flexor met or exceeded the isometric torque magnitude of the Gait2392 biceps femoris short head, and the extensor met or exceeded that of the vastus medialis. These tests extend earlier work on geometric attachment placement \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019,bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020} by checking the torque each route delivers under load.

In a pulley-assisted BPA route, a fixed pulley redirects tendon tension. A multi-part tackle also changes the relation between actuator travel and insertion force and needs space for the moving pulleys (Appendix~\ref{sec:app_routing_extensions}). A cam or artificial patella can change the moment arm as the knee flexes. To test that design, I would measure knee-axis torque and tendon tension on both sides of the contact across a knee-angle sweep. Recording the angles at which the tendon engages and leaves the cam would show where any discrepancy from the predicted torque occurs.

Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. Its timing and magnitude distinguish a knee that supplies energy during extension from one that resists motion to absorb a landing load. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.

In the SADb a researcher can trace a proposed connection to the stimulus and response that support it, then compare the preparations in which the response changed. In the Table view, selecting \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} under \emph{Pathway} returns linked papers. The record for \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} opens a curation note, its pathway links, and the article DOI. In decerebrate cats, stimulating the plantaris nerve inhibited medial gastrocnemius motoneurons at rest. During the extensor phase of midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion, the same stimulation excited these synergist motoneurons. In an acute spinal preparation treated with clonidine, inhibition decreased without the short-latency excitation. The record also links to \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition}. Reading the original experiment shows why those two links belong together and why a controller designer would test a state-dependent group~I pathway. The stimulation recruited group~I afferents and did not isolate Ib input.

The monthly literature watch supplies candidates for manual curation (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_methods}). For a pathway such as extensor group~I excitation, the most useful addition to a record would be a direct link from each reported sign to its preparation, stimulus, and phase. A reader could then distinguish a measured reversal from an assumption in a computational model before following their citation links. The Bubble map already identifies citation communities by color. Grouping their papers spatially would provide a second way to locate related studies \citep{bolen_using_2024}.

Morrow and I first transferred the Deng controller to the Li walker in AnimatLab. The legs cycled while suspended and the model tipped when released. The result motivated a practical change in how I tested controllers. I built tools to follow one signal from sensory input through the neural circuit to actuator force and joint motion. In the knee example an extensor Ia pulse produces a measurable extension and recovery. In the supported W2L model, removing the specified sensory inputs and conductances displaced footfalls from antiphase while the body continued to move forward. Recording both contact and movement made the coordination deficit observable.

The human-model drive experiment tested a different dependence. The human model continued to step in place under its support rig with the supplementary left and right hand-drive channels set to zero and the shared descending drive still active. A separate W2L robot model progressed with reduced supplementary drive under its harness (Section~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}). These tests identify which command was removed and what mechanical support the remaining controller had to work against.

A next controller-transfer test would stimulate the same RG, PF, or MN pathway under prescribed sensory replay and during closed-loop motion. A phase shift at the rhythm generator would distinguish a reset from a skipped motor burst with preserved rhythm (Section~\ref{sec:app_layer_stimulus}). Physiological and modeling studies provide reference responses for such experiments \citep{selionov_tonic_2009,rybak_modelling_2006,markin_afferent_2010,shevtsova_modeling_2016}. Repeating the protocol with the same unaffected synaptic gains, mechanical support, and perturbation would locate where the responses diverge.

For the biped I would first test whether an estimate of trunk orientation and angular velocity improves recovery from a repeatable disturbance at fixed harness assistance. Adding a visual reference in a second condition would test the effect of correcting inertial drift under the same disturbance. The expected contribution of each signal depends on the task \citep{akay_relative_2021}. Figure~\ref{fig:sensorium_hierarchy} places these proposed pathways above the implemented spinal network.

Once spinal timing is repeatable, adaptive step length provides an observable task for a higher-level controller. A useful first comparison would measure the size and persistence of the correction to a repeated perturbation with and without the proposed adaptive pathway.

My longer-term goal is a robot that can perform a kickflip. The knee must deliver power during takeoff, the controller must estimate orientation in the air, and the legs must absorb energy when contact resumes. Those are three identifiable experiments on the way from a stationary torque measurement to a coordinated whole-body maneuver.

The four contributions make it possible to ask where a proposed controller and a particular leg first disagree. A force shortfall at a known pressure points to actuator or route mechanics. Correct force with a mistimed footfall points to recruitment, sensory encoding, or the support condition. The measurements and interventions developed here allow those explanations to be tested separately.

Support is part of the experimental apparatus. A suspension spring can isolate air-stage limb motion, and rails or a harness can permit ground contact while constraining the torso. I report the force definition, denominator, and scored interval for each ground result. For example, one supported Gait2392 recording averaged \qty{48.848}{\percent} net superior force relative to a \qty{768.756726}{\newton} moving-model weight, and \qty{115.561}{\newton} RMS horizontal restraint over \qtyrange{5}{13}{\second} (4,001 samples). The two measurements describe different actions of the same apparatus.

In the historical BPA-interface experiment, the nominal support setting was \qty{70}{\percent} of a \qty{411}{\newton} model weight and peak commanded pressure was \qty{372}{\kPa}. It exercised the quasi-static BPA command-to-force interface. Suspended motion of the converted robot with Hill-type muscles and supported CAD motion with ideal reference tensions are separate demonstrations.

The robot drive-weaning configuration progressed \qty{1.72}{\meter} in \qty{30}{\second}, retained progression at \qty{60}{\percent} of the supplementary drive scale, and passed twelve perturbed repeats. Mechanical support remained in place, and contact duty fell below the strict walking criterion. The human model retained bilateral stepping in place under the support rig after the added left/right hand-drive channels were removed, with \qty{2.0773}{\nano\ampere} still applied through the shared locomotor-drive input. No harness-free walking was established in these experiments.

After correcting how the evaluator delivered saved per-target gains, I replayed a separate W2L configuration in four independent \qty{30}{\second} trials. The trajectories were identical. During $4.5\leq t<30$\,s, 28 left and 21 right primary heel strikes gave a median left-strike phase of 0.496 between successive right strikes, and forward displacement was \qty{2.246}{\meter}. A separate speed fit used $8\leq t<30$\,s and gave \qty{0.0918}{\meter\per\second}. All twelve independent \qty{1}{\percent} parameter perturbations passed the supported-stepping criterion.

Setting nominal constant weight support to zero left the position-control harness active. Its mean vertical force over $4.5\leq t<30$\,s was approximately \qty{16.75}{\percent} of the legacy \qty{411}{\newton} weight. The walker repeated its supported stepping with this force, although contact duty remained below the strict walking criterion.

For the sensory intervention I set nominal weight support to 0.25 and compared the intact controller with deletions at the same drive, mechanical support, and remaining fitted parameters. The evaluator applies a common \qty{40}{\newton} forward push at $8\leq t<8.15$\,s, including in the intact condition. The separately named forward-push file reproduces all of the control's saved arrays and thus supplies no unforced comparison. Each new neural input is held for \qty{2}{\milli\second}, spanning two \qty{1}{\milli\second} physics steps.

The combined sensory deletion set 35 nonzero fitted parameters to zero, including the contact and pooled-Ib input amplitudes, heel-cascade and crossed-heel connections, and Ia-, II-, and Ib-labeled projections to rhythm, pattern, and segmental pathways. All sixteen external contact and Ib input currents then remained zero. In the separate Ib-only deletion the twelve Ib inputs went to zero and the contact currents remained. The comparison tests the contribution of the specified set of sensory inputs and connections to bilateral coordination.

I counted primary heel strikes over $4.5\leq t<30$\,s from rising crossings above \qty{20}{\newton}, accepting successive strikes on the same side only when they were more than \qty{0.45}{\second} apart. Median phase locates a left strike between two successive right strikes. The historical criterion required a finite trial without a fall, at least six strikes per side, phase in $[0.35,0.65]$, and forward displacement greater than \qty{0.05}{\meter}. The intact condition yielded 34 left and 22 right strikes, phase 0.498, and \qty{2.239}{\meter} progression. The combined deletion yielded 20 left and 31 right strikes and \qty{1.996}{\meter} progression, but its phase of 0.223 failed alternation. Ib-only deletion yielded 19 left and 20 right strikes, phase 0.494, and \qty{2.302}{\meter}. Fresh replays reproduced all 15 numerical trajectory arrays for each condition.

Mild and strong drive reductions, reversal to a \qty{40}{\newton} backward push, and individual Ia, Ib, Renshaw, crossed-heel, and heel-cascade deletions retained the historical supported-stepping criterion. Renshaw deletion reduced forward displacement to \qty{0.081}{\meter}, and commissural deletion failed bilateral stepping. Heel-strike phase, progression, and continued joint cycling thus distinguished interventions that a count of moving limbs alone would group together.

At contact handover I used measured normal load $F$ to phase in muscle support. For $u=\operatorname{clip}[(F-F_0)/(F_1-F_0),0,1]$, contact confidence is $c=u^2(3-2u)$ with nominal thresholds $F_0=\qty{1}{\newton}$ and $F_1=\qty{5}{\newton}$. The allocator normalizes its phase preferences, multiplies by confidence, filters the requested support with a \qty{10}{\milli\second} time constant, and limits the request to the current confidence. The resulting targets act through the muscles. The external harness force is measured separately.

During swing, the allocator uses minimum foot-mesh height and time since the RG swing event to request lift through hip and knee torque targets. Its velocity feedback acts on the lift task. Root and distal-foot coordinates are excluded, and physical joint damping is unchanged. All 26 saved numerical arrays agreed in the independent repeat and reference-backend replay. The model, route, controller, and dependency hashes matched, and compiling the geometry again reproduced the foot heights. The original compiled binary is unavailable. Five of eight local perturbations passed. The other three reached the predictive knee margin, as did the lower-support trials. Soft-contact penetrations reached \qtylist{16.13;12.91}{\milli\meter}.
